country.comment: Empirical data come from Round 7 of the Afrobarometer across 34 African countries (2016-2018). Guinea and Mauritius are mentioned in Section 4 as illustrative sample countries; country-by-country summary statistics are in online Appendix Table A1.
country.where_found: PDF p. 2, Section 1; PDF pp. 7-8, Section 4

effect_estimate.comment: All main estimates are probit or ordered probit marginal effects with country fixed effects and region-clustered standard errors. Regional utility corruption reduces clean-water access specifically where piped infrastructure exists, whereas individual bribery predicts having an in-house/compound water source without improving reliable clean-water access.
effect_estimate.value: In binary probit models of household clean-water access (Access = 1 if not 'always' going without enough clean water), regional incidence of utilities corruption has a negative marginal effect of -0.15 (SE = 0.073, p < 0.05, N = 44,887) and -0.16 controlling for individual bribery (SE = 0.073, p < 0.05, N = 44,778; moving from 0% to 70% regional corruption reduces access likelihood by ~10 percentage points; 1 SD increase reduces access by 0.5 percentage points). Splitting by area infrastructure, the negative association holds only in areas with a piped water system (-0.14, SE = 0.045, p < 0.01, N = 24,511) and is null in areas without pipes (-0.12, SE = 0.158, not significant, N = 20,267). Individual bribery for utilities has no statistically significant association with clean-water access in binary probit (-0.01, SE = 0.007 in Col. 1; -0.00, SE = 0.006 in Col. 3, N = 44,778), though in ordered probit (N = 44,778) regional utility corruption reduces 'Never' going without clean water by -0.4272 (SE = 0.1860, p < 0.05) and increases 'Always' going without by 0.1095 (SE = 0.0481, p < 0.05), while individual bribery reduces 'Never' by -0.0257 (SE = 0.0129, p < 0.10). Conversely, having paid a bribe for utilities significantly increases the probability of having a nominal water source inside the house or compound by 0.06 (SE = 0.018, p < 0.01, N = 44,546; ordered probit: +0.0253 inside house, +0.0186 inside compound, -0.0439 outside compound, all p < 0.01), whereas regional utility corruption has no statistically significant effect on source location (-0.26, SE = 0.202).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Cross-sectional observational survey design appraised with JBI has a maximum ceiling of 2; rated 1 (documented statistical association) because the study tests statistical associations between self-reported individual/regional utility bribery (which spans water, sanitation, and electricity) and household water outcomes, while inferring rather than directly observing utility officials' administrative and operational degradation of piped systems.

mechanism_flags.comment: Empirical predictors measure informal payments/bribes, gifts, or favors required by government officials to obtain utility services (fees/BURDEN) and the paper analyzes corrupt exercise of provider autonomy/discretion in service delivery and connections (discretion/DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION); institutional fragmentation and repair delays are also discussed theoretically in Sections 1-3 and 6.
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 6-8, Sections 3-4; PDF p. 12, Section 5.1

outcome_flags.comment: Primary outcome measures how often over the past year the household went without enough clean water for home use (capturing water_access, service_quality, service_quantity, and service_reliability), and secondary outcome Homesource measures whether the main water access point/connection is inside the house, inside the compound, or outside the compound (capturing formal_connection / physical connectivity to water infrastructure).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Quantitative observational cross-sectional household survey regression analysis (Afrobarometer Round 7) without a quasi-experimental intervention comparator; authors explicitly state they rely on cross-sectional data and do not make causal claims.
risk_of_bias_tool.value: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

sample_size.comment: Individual respondents (one per sampled household) across 34 African countries in Afrobarometer Round 7, with standard errors clustered by survey region.
sample_size.value: 44,778 respondents/households in main analytical sample (44,887 observations in models without individual bribery; 24,511 observations in piped-water areas and 20,267 in non-piped areas; 44,546 observations in water source location models)

study_design.comment: Observational cross-sectional multi-country survey analysis using Afrobarometer Round 7 CAPI data; online appendix also reports multilevel mixed-effects robustness models and comparisons with Rounds 5 and 6.
study_design.value: Cross-sectional multi-country household survey analysis (Afrobarometer Round 7, 2016-2018) using binary probit and ordered probit regression models with country fixed effects and region-clustered standard errors
